rows.verified: Lift-truck operators must receive training to the standards described in the L117 Approved Code of Practice.
Lift-truck operator training should include basic training, specific job training and familiarisation training.
Basic and specific job training should take place away from production pressure, while familiarisation should occur on the job under close supervision.
Even occasional operators of covered rider-operated lift trucks must meet the applicable minimum training standard.
Industrial lift trucks require thorough examination under LOLER and PUWER, separate from routine preventive maintenance or servicing.
Lift-truck safety arrangements should address safe use, pedestrian protection, maintenance and thorough examination.
Conversion training is needed before an operator uses a materially different truck type or attachment without suitable prior training.
Site controllers should ensure visiting drivers or service personnel operating lift trucks are adequately trained and familiar with site and machine risks.
The required controls depend on truck type, attachment, load, surface, slopes, visibility, pedestrian interaction and operating environment.
Lift-truck evidence is equipment-, load-, operator- and site-specific and is not an exact parcel-level accident probability.
Warehouse risk management should address manual handling, moving vehicles, mechanical handling, working at height and accident procedures.
High-risk manual lifting should be avoided where possible, including through palletising or redesigning packages.
Mechanical aids such as pallet trucks, roller conveyors, hoists, scissor lifts and suitable trolleys should be considered to reduce handling risk.
Warehouse risk assessments should account for periods when vehicle or pedestrian traffic changes, such as shift changes.
Loading, transport and unloading risks must be managed to protect workers and members of the public.
Goods transported on or in vehicles must be secured, and loads should be stable at the point of loading.
Loading areas need sufficient space and suitable arrangements for safe loading and unloading.
Pallet selection, condition, loading and storage arrangements must be suitable for the loads and racking system used.
Warehouse controls depend on goods, racking, handling methods, traffic, staffing, facility layout and operating peaks.
Warehousing evidence is facility-, stock- and activity-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
